problem: LLM/VLM navigation systems for people with visual impairments (PVI) rely on precise explicit user commands or dense maps (3D point clouds, SLAM) that are expensive for an LLM to process, and rule-based assistive aids lack adaptivity, hazard reasoning and personalization.
motivation: PVI find it hard to describe destinations or landmarks, and dense-map LLM processing causes delays. A compact text map with straight paths and right-angle turns (easier for PVI) lets an LLM plan globally with commonsense reasoning for safety and personalization.
key_idea: Represent the environment as a hand-built text-based topological graph (nodes at intersections, edges with distance and direction, straight segments and right-angle turns) that a GPT-4o agent plans over via a path-planning module, with CLIP image retrieval for localization and recovery.
insight: A path-planning module that feeds only the relevant route text is essential: removing it and giving the full text map drops success from 86% to 40% (context overload), and removing the system prompt gives 0%. Model scale matters strongly: GPT-4o 84/86% vs Llama 3.2 11B 20/24% and Qwen2.5-VL-7B 0/4%, with failures from forgetting commands or confusing turn directions.
method: Text-based topological map: an occupancy grid with manually placed nodes at intersections, turns and decision points forms a directed weighted graph; edges carry distance d_ij and direction θ_ij, restricted to straight paths and right-angle turns
Agent: GPT-4o with a system prompt interprets the user query and outputs high-level plans, image query commands and user responses
Path planning module: processes the text map on a navigation query and returns a textual route description, allowing multiple routes to be compared and adapted to hazards or preferences

Embedding module and two vector databases: off-the-shelf CLIP embeds images with location/orientation metadata; a static main database of the whole environment and a secondary, updatable navigation database

Topological navigation and localization: at each node or turn, cosine similarity between the current observation and the retrieved node image is checked against a threshold; a low score triggers a fallback search of the main database to re-localize
Low-level planner: converts the agent's decisions into feasible robot motions and reports the distance travelled on arrival at a node
Commonsense hazard reasoning and personalization: the LLM warns about hazards such as wet floors and proposes alternative routes, and adapts routes, speed and dialogue style to user preferences

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen, API); also compared Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.2 Vision 90B/11B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B; CLIP for embeddings
setting.observation: egocentric RGB images (matched by CLIP embeddings), no depth
setting.action_space: high-level text commands (go straight distance / turn 90°) converted by a low-level planner to robot motion along topological nodes
setting.privileged: hand-built, pre-labeled text topological map and pre-labeled image database with location/orientation metadata; user start location inferred from images

numbers_note: Custom simulated evaluations only, no standard benchmark; no SPL or NE reported. The ablation table reference points to the model comparison table.
results: GPT-4o reaches 84% (house) and 86% (office) success, beating Claude 3.5 Sonnet (74/78%) and Llama 3.2 Vision 90B (76/74%). It detects 90% of kidnapped-robot errors and recovers from 72%, detects hazards in 25/30 hazardous trials (10/30 false alarms on harmless objects), and reaches 92% success on preference-based routing.
limitations: Only simulated tests in iGibson, with no real-world trials or participants with visual impairments
Text map is built manually and needs pre-labeled images; depends on cloud LLMs, and long route lists can exceed the context window
Hazard detection lacks depth/height awareness, and localization fails in feature-sparse or visually similar corridors
